chapters.title: Chapter 9 · My Lord Bag of Rice
chapters.artPrompt: a brave young warrior standing firm on a great arched bridge over a wide lake at dusk as a huge dragon lies coiled across the planks, mist and lantern lights on the far water, a mountain shaped like a sleeping centipede behind, deep blue evening with warm gold, heroic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago a brave young warrior named Hidesato set out to see the world. He walked all day, and at evening came to a great bridge over Lake Biwa. Across the bridge, coiled from end to end, lay a huge dragon. Hidesato did not turn back. He stepped over the great coils calmly, as if stepping over a fallen log. He was a good archer, and carried a bow and three arrows.

Then the dragon changed into a gentle old man in wonderful robes, and bowed low. “I am the Dragon King of Lake Biwa,” he said. “A monstrous centipede lives on the mountain. Every year it kills some of my children. Only a hero can end it. Will you help us?” His old eyes were full of tears as he said it.

Hidesato went up the mountain that night and waited in the dark. The centipede came down the slope like a moving line of lanterns, with two eyes like burning suns. He had but three arrows. The first two glanced off its hundred legs. Then he spat upon the head of the last arrow, took aim at a shining scale near the creature's head, and let it fly.
The hundred-legged centipede comes down the mountain like lanterns.
New word: centipede — a long, creeping creature with very many legs. This one had a hundred!

The centipede fell, and the mountain was still. The whole lake kingdom kept a feast that night. The Dragon King heaped gifts upon his guest: a bag of rice that never gave out, a roll of silk that never shortened, and chests of treasure besides. And from that day, people called the happy warrior My Lord Bag of Rice. And Hidesato never wanted for rice again all his days.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Bamboo-Cutter and the Moon-Child
chapters.artPrompt: an old bamboo-cutter kneeling in a moonlit grove holding a tiny shining girl found inside a split bamboo stalk, fireflies and tall bamboo stems all around, the full moon huge and gentle above, silver-blue night with pearl glow, magical storybook illustration

blocks.text: An old bamboo-cutter was working in his grove one bright, moonlit night, when one bamboo stalk shone strangely from inside. He cut it open — and there sat a tiny girl, lovely as a pearl. He carried her home to his old wife, and they brought her up as their own child. They thought her a gift from heaven, and so she was.

The little girl grew into the loveliest maiden in Japan, and people called her the Shining Princess. Five noblemen begged to marry her. So she set them each an impossible task: the stone bowl of Buddha from India, a robe of fire-rat fur, a jewel from a dragon's neck. Some tried to cheat, and some tried to buy, and every one of them failed.

At last the Emperor himself asked her to come to the palace. She refused gently, but they became true friends all the same, and wrote letters for many seasons. Yet she had a secret. She had come from the moon — and to the moon she must return. And the fifteenth night of the eighth month was drawing near.
On the full-moon night, beings of cloud come down for the Shining Princess.
New word: elixir — a magic drink that is supposed to give long life.

On the night of the full moon, cloud-borne beings came down, and she put on a robe that took away all sorrow, and rose with them into the sky. She left the Emperor a letter and a little vial of elixir. He would not live forever without her. He ordered the vial burned on the highest mountain in Japan, and the smoke rose toward the moon for years. That mountain is called Fuji to this day.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The White Hare and the Crocodiles
chapters.artPrompt: a small white hare running happily along the backs of a long row of grey crocodiles lying like a bridge across bright blue sea, distant green shore of Inaba ahead, white gulls above, sparkling morning light, playful sunny storybook illustration

blocks.text: A little white hare longed to cross the sea to the land of Inaba. He was too small to swim so far, but he was not called clever for nothing. “Crocodiles love to boast of their great numbers,” he said. So he called to the crocodiles: “Let us count your tribe! Lie in a row from here to the shore, and I will run along your backs and count you one by one.”

The proud crocodiles lay in a long line, and the hare ran across, counting, counting, till the very last one. Then he could not keep his tongue still. “I tricked you, you silly crocodiles!” he cried. The angry crocodiles caught him and stripped off his soft white fur, and left him weeping on the beach. He hopped to the sand and looked at himself, and wished he had kept his tongue still.

Eighty great gods came walking by. “Bathe in the sea, and let the wind dry you,” they said, laughing at his sore skin. That made the poor hare burn all the more. Then came the youngest god, kind and quiet. “Wash in fresh water,” he said, “and roll in soft cattail fluff, and you will be yourself again.” The eighty gods laughed, and went on their grand way.
The kind young god helps the hare at the fresh-water pool.
Ask your child: the hare was clever, but was he kind? What happened when a trick turned into boasting?

The hare bathed and rolled in the soft fluff, and his white coat grew again, as soft as before. “Go on to Inaba,” said the hare. “You shall win the princess there.” And so it came true: the kind young god won the princess, and the white hare went home happy — and never boasted again.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Mirror of Matsuyama
chapters.artPrompt: a gentle girl kneeling by a paper lantern opening a round mirror in a lacquer case, her father and stepmother watching softly behind, the face in the mirror glowing like a memory, tatami room with sliding doors open to a garden, warm lamplight with cool moonlight, tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago in Matsuyama there lived a good man, his wife, and their little daughter. One day the father had to make a long journey to the great city, and the girl wept to see him go. “You shall keep something of mine,” he said, and gave her a round mirror in a lacquer case. “Look in it whenever you think of me.” She carried the mirror everywhere in her sleeve, like a treasure.

Her mother fell ill and died before her father came home. Lonely and sad, the girl would open the mirror's case — and there, always, was her mother's own face, for she had grown to be very like her. She kept the mirror hidden as her greatest treasure, and said her little prayers beside it every night. Looking at it made her feel less alone.

When the father returned, he married again. The new wife grew jealous of the quiet girl and her secret meetings with something in a box. What could the child be hiding? “She is bewitched,” the stepmother whispered. “She shuts herself away with some dark magic night after night.”
The girl shows her father the mirror, and he sees his lost wife's face.
Ask your child: what did the daughter really see in the mirror? Why did it comfort her?

The father asked for the mirror. The girl opened it, hiding nothing, and there looked out his dead wife's gentle face. Then he understood his daughter's heart, and the stepmother understood too, and there was peace in the house from that day on. The mirror was treasured like a jewel, and the story of the mirror of Matsuyama is told to children in Japan still, and the mirror stayed bright and clear in the family for generations.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · The Story of Princess Hase
chapters.artPrompt: a graceful young woman in flowing robes playing a biwa lute inside a great temple hall while an old white-haired prince listens with tears and recognition, tall candles and gold screen behind, shafts of morning light through the doorway, gentle golden-hued storybook illustration

blocks.text: A brave prince and his wife had no child, and grieved for it. They prayed at the old temple of Hase, and in time a little daughter was born. They named her Hase, for the temple, and loved her more than words can say. She grew up gentle and clever, and played the biwa, an old silvery lute, more sweetly than anyone in the province.

Then her mother died, and in time a stepmother came to the house, and she wanted everything for herself. At a feast one day, a cup of poisoned wine was passed, and the wicked stepmother cried out that the princess had done it. The prince, half-mad with grief and doubt, believed the lie. He would not kill his own child, but he set her adrift on the sea in a little boat, with only her biwa for company.

The sea was kind to her. Fishermen found the little boat and took the princess in, and in a far place she lived quietly, known only as a wonderful player of the biwa. Years passed, and her father grew old and full of sorrow. One day, at a great temple service, he heard a biwa played like no other on earth.
The old prince hears the biwa, and knows his lost daughter at last.
New word: biwa — a Japanese lute with a round body and sweet strings.

He followed the music — and there, playing, was his own Hase. Then all the truth came out: the poisoned cup, the lie, the little boat. The stepmother was sent away in disgrace, and the prince never let his daughter out of his sight again. She had suffered much, and it had made her music kind.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · The Story of the Man Who Did Not Wish to Die
chapters.artPrompt: a comfortable shopkeeper waking from sleep beside his own singing kettle in a small warm wine shop, morning light through the paper screen, a dream of sea voyage and a pearl-like pill fading above him like mist, cosy amber light, gentle comic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Sentaro kept a wine shop, and he was comfortable in every way but one: he was afraid of dying. He thought about it at his meals, and at his work, and in his sleep. His shop did well, and his kettle sang from morning to night. One night a wandering sage from China came to his door, and Sentaro begged him for the elixir of life. “In my country lives Jofuku, who found it long ago,” said the sage. “Go and find him, if you are not afraid of the sea.”

Sentaro sailed at once. He searched city after city, and at last he was given the elixir, a little pill like a pearl. He took it — and found himself living on and on. A hundred years, and his old neighbours were dust. Five hundred, and even his own memory was tired. Kings rose and fell, and fashions changed a hundred times, and he stayed on. Never to die, he learned, is a strange and lonely wish.

“Let me be a common man again,” he cried, “with one short, sweet life!” And then he woke. There was his own shop, his own kettle singing, his own ordinary morning. It had all been a dream, from the moment the sage knocked at his door.
Sentaro wakes beside his own kettle, glad to be a common man.
Ask your child: Sentaro wished for endless life. Why did he change his mind? What is good about a life that has an end?

After that, Sentaro lived his days one by one, and found them sweet. When neighbours praised his cheerfulness, he only smiled. He still dreamed of the elixir sometimes, the tale says — but never again on purpose, and never in the daytime. And he lived long and happily, as common men do.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · The Story of Prince Yamato Take
chapters.artPrompt: a young prince in hunting robes swinging a shining sword to cut a wide green path through a burning moor, walls of flame and smoke on every side, wind-blown sparks against a deep orange sky, heroic sweeping storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago there was a prince of Japan named Yamato, as bold as a young eagle. The wild robber-braves of the south were brothers, and no one dared face them, so the prince went himself. He was still almost a boy, but his heart was a lion's heart. He slipped into their great feast dressed as a dancing girl, and the robbers, loud with wine, never dreamed what the quiet dancer carried.

When the feast was at its wildest, the dancer threw off her sleeves — and it was the prince! Before the robbers could reach their weapons, both were beaten, and the south country was at peace. On the way home, Yamato stopped at a great shrine, where his aunt kept the sacred sword. “Take it,” she said. “It has served heroes before you.”

His greatest adventure came on a wide moor, where a wicked chief set the dry grass on fire to burn him alive. Flames ran at him from every side. Then Yamato drew the sacred sword and mowed a green path through the grass, as a mower mows a field, and stood safe where the fire could not touch him. The moor burned for a day, and the wicked chief gained nothing by it. Ever after, the sword was called the Grass-Mower.
Yamato mows a green path through the ring of fire.
New word: shrine — a holy place. Yamato's sword was kept in a shrine until he needed it.

He had many more adventures by sea and by land, and grew weary at last, as heroes do. But his name is remembered in Japan as one of the bravest of princes. The Grass-Mower still rests among the imperial treasures, where poets go to think of him.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 · The Green Willow
chapters.artPrompt: a gentle maiden in pale green robes waving farewell beside a young samurai at the door of a tiny cottage under a great old willow tree, drifting willow leaves turning to light around her, misty green valley at dusk, soft melancholy tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: A young samurai was travelling in the hills when a great storm caught him in the dark. Through the rain he saw the glow of a fire in a little cottage under an old willow tree. A gentle maiden lived there, and made him welcome by her fire, and would not hear of his going on in such weather. Her house was as neat as a shell, and her fire never seemed to go out.

The storm lasted three days, and the maiden's quiet company lasted longer. The samurai forgot the road he had been travelling, and asked to stay forever. They were married under the willow, and their little home was the happiest in the valley. The villagers called them the luckiest pair in the whole valley. But sometimes the maiden looked at the old tree with strange, soft eyes.

“Promise me one thing,” she said at last. “Whatever happens, do not grieve too much for me. My life is bound up with that willow.” He promised — and laughed at his own uneasiness, for the tree had stood a hundred years, and would stand a hundred more.
The maiden of the green willow waves farewell, growing pale as a leaf.
New word: bound up — tied closely together. The maiden's life was tied to the tree, like a leaf to its branch.

Then men came with axes, for the old willow was marked to be cut down. When the great tree fell, the maiden's hand grew cold in his, and she faded away like a leaf on the wind. The samurai mourned her all his days. And the people of that valley still say that when the wind stirs the green willows, a gentle maiden is walking there, and the wind in the leaves sounds softly like her voice.
